questions.stem: How does Hierarchical Data Modelling structure data?
options: In a strict tree where each child record has exactly one parent
In owner–member sets allowing many parents per record
In nodes and edges with typed relationships
In JSON documents with nested arrays
In fact and dimension tables
questions.explanation: Hierarchical modelling uses a strict tree-like format in which each child has exactly one parent, forming a single-rooted hierarchy of one-to-many relationships.

questions.stem: Which mainframe system is given as the classic example of hierarchical data modelling in the 1960s and 1970s?
options: CODASYL IDMS
IBM's Information Management System (IMS)
ObjectStore
Neo4j
Cassandra
questions.explanation: The hierarchical model dominated the 1960s and 1970s in mainframe environments such as IBM's Information Management System (IMS).

questions.stem: In the hierarchical loan example Bank → Branch → Loan Officer → Customer → Loan → Repayment, what is true of a Repayment record?
options: It can belong to several loans at once
It is stored independently of any loan
It cannot exist without a Loan
It is the root of the hierarchy
It links directly to a Branch
questions.explanation: Each child depends entirely on its parent in a hierarchy: a Repayment cannot exist without a Loan, and a Loan cannot exist without a Customer.

questions.stem: Why is retrieving all repayments for a specific loan straightforward in a hierarchical model?
options: Because the database performs a declarative join
Because repayments are stored in a separate fact table
Because the query engine infers the relationship semantically
Because the system simply navigates down the predefined tree path
Because repayments are indexed by customer
questions.explanation: Traversal along hierarchical branches is fast because relationships are physically structured according to the access pattern, so the system navigates down the tree.

questions.stem: Which query illustrates the kind of question a strict hierarchical model struggles to answer?
options: Which repayments belong to loan L001?
Which customers belong to this loan officer?
Which loans belong to this customer?
Which branches belong to this bank?
Which loan officers approved loans across multiple branches?
questions.explanation: In a strict tree a Loan Officer belongs to only one Branch, so cross-branch, many-to-many questions are difficult or impossible to represent naturally.

questions.stem: Why does normalisation theory not apply to hierarchical data modelling?
options: Because the model predates the relational model and is based on physical navigation paths rather than dependency theory
Because hierarchical databases are always already in 3NF
Because hierarchical models have no keys
Because hierarchical databases store only unstructured text
Because normalisation applies only to NoSQL systems
questions.explanation: The hierarchical model predates the relational model; its structure is determined by hierarchical rules and navigation paths, so concepts such as 3NF or BCNF are irrelevant.

questions.stem: Where does hierarchical data modelling still exist today?
options: In most new cloud-native enterprise systems
In legacy mainframes and directory services such as LDAP and Active Directory
In data warehouses built as star schemas
In graph databases for fraud detection
In event-streaming platforms
questions.explanation: Hierarchical modelling is largely obsolete for new enterprise systems but survives in legacy mainframes and directory services such as LDAP and Active Directory.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between Hierarchical Data Modelling and a taxonomy?
options: A taxonomy has no parent–child relationships
A hierarchical model is drawn as a graph while a taxonomy is drawn as a tree
A hierarchical model is a database storage model governing physical access, whereas a taxonomy is a conceptual classification of meaning
A taxonomy is used only in mainframes
They are the same thing under different names
questions.explanation: In hierarchical databases the tree is the physical access path to data; in taxonomies the tree is a conceptual structure used to classify knowledge and add meaning.

questions.stem: Which example illustrates a taxonomy rather than a hierarchical database structure?
options: Bank → Branch → Loan → Repayment
Customer → Loan → Officer traversal
Owner–member sets in IDMS
Loan → Personal Loan → Student Loan
LoanID → CustID → CustomerName
questions.explanation: Loan → Personal Loan → Student Loan classifies types of loan for semantic clarity; it does not dictate how data is physically stored.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a strength of hierarchical data modelling?
options: High efficiency for predictable one-to-many queries
Simple, understandable structures when relationships are strictly nested
Strong performance in tightly controlled operational systems with fixed access patterns
Deterministic navigation from parent to child
Effective support for dynamic, ad-hoc analytical queries
questions.explanation: Hierarchical modelling lacks flexibility, struggles with many-to-many relationships and does not support dynamic or ad-hoc analytical queries effectively.
